name: Law of Common Region
description: Elements enclosed within the same bounded area are perceived as belonging together. Containers, cards, shaded panels, and section backgrounds all exploit this grouping cue in interface design.
design_relevance_note: Directly informs layout systems that use cards, panels, grouped form sections, pricing boxes, and shaded regions to signal which elements belong together.
prevalence_note: Dedicated Laws of UX entry and a standard visual-grouping principle in UI/layout teaching (cards, panels, containers), especially in visual and product-design practice.

findings.description: Elements located within the same bounded region of space are perceived as grouped together; in Palmer's demonstrations this common-region cue strongly influenced grouping judgments, could override proximity and similarity, and depended on perceived depth relations and hierarchical embedding.
findings.source_title: Common region: A new principle of perceptual grouping

applications.title: An older Food Network tablet app's recipe list became ambiguous without common-region grouping
applications.description: Nielsen Norman Group's Aurora Harley describes a real usability problem in an older version of the Food Network tablet app: large gaps existed between elements associated with the same recipe (likely left to accommodate multi-line titles), and the result was that it became unclear which byline and rating belonged to which recipe -- the one above the gap or the one below. The article's stated fix is straightforward: enclosing all the related content for one recipe within a single visible boundary (a common region) removes the ambiguity, since a shared border or background immediately signals which elements belong together regardless of the whitespace between them.
applications.ethical_note: A usability-clarity fix (reducing ambiguity about which byline/rating belongs to which recipe) that purely benefits users, with no persuasive or manipulative dimension.

applications.title: Slack uses a dark background region to separate app chrome from message content
applications.description: Nielsen Norman Group's article on the principle of common region describes how the Slack app uses a dark background color to group together all of the surrounding UI controls (search, navigation, workspace switcher, channel list) as a single common region, visually distinguishing that 'chrome' from the lighter message-content area. Within that same dark region, thin dividing lines further create common sub-regions -- separating search/navigation at the top from the workspace list on the far left and the channel list within a workspace -- so users can tell at a glance which controls belong to which functional group.
applications.ethical_note: A structural clarity technique that helps users parse the interface faster, with no persuasive or manipulative dimension.
